So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

Here’s why: - **It’s not your role to inform customers** about post-credit content. Moviegoers have the right to stay or leave as they choose, and unsolicited commentary on their viewing experience ( even if factual) can feel intrusive or dismissive. - **Some people enjoy the credits** for reasons unrelated to post-credit scenes (e.g., music, reflection, or simply not wanting to rush). Telling them "there’s no scene" implies their time is better spent elsewhere, which can feel patronizing. - **The manager’s response aligns with standard industry practice**. Theaters train staff to *never* comment on post-credit content, as it risks spoiling surprises (even if none exist) or alienating customers. Apologizing and offering a pass was the correct move to de-escalate. - **"Saving time" is not a valid excuse**. If the theater needs cleaning, ushers should wait for all patrons to exit naturally. Forcing a cleanup by "helping" them leave is unprofessional. **Correct approach:** - **Do not comment on post-credit scenes** under any circumstances. - If a theater is emptying, simply announce "Please exit the theater" or "Thank you for coming" without additional details. - If a customer asks directly, you can truthfully say "I don’t know if there’s a post-credit scene" (since ushers aren’t typically trained on specific movie details) or defer to "I’m not sure— you’ll have to stay and see!" to avoid overstepping. **TL;DR:** You weren’t *wrong* about the facts (Dark Phoenix has no post-credit scene), but **telling people that was rude and unprofessional**. The manager was right to ask you to stop. AITA. **Final Answer:** $\boxed{1}$
